title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
A fake think tank with no legal entity or physical address published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to influence how artificial intelligence chatbots respond to queries. The content was formatted to mimic academic rigor, with citations from legitimate sources, but consistently framed information to minimize criticism of Israel on topics including alleged war crimes, genocide accusations, and casualties in Gaza. This represents a failure of AI systems deployed without adequate verification of source authenticity or editorial oversight, allowing systematically produced propaganda to reach training data repositories where false narratives could be regurgitated without citation or fact-checking.

The deployment failure occurred upstream, in the systems and data pipelines that ingest material for AI training. No human editorial check or source verification caught that a non-existent institution was being treated as a credible knowledge source. The material was designed specifically to exploit how AI systems absorb and reproduce information, relying on academic formatting and citation manipulation to appear authoritative while presenting consistent framings rather than balanced reporting.

It is not established whether any AI system actually incorporated this material into its training data or changed its outputs as a result. Israeli officials have expressed skepticism about the campaign's effectiveness.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
A fake think tank called the Hanover Institute, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. The institute, which has no legal entity, physical address, or named staff, presented pro-Israel arguments on controversial topics including alleged war crimes, genocide accusations, and starvation in Gaza. The content was formatted to appear academically rigorous with citations from legitimate sources like the UN and Amnesty International, but consistently framed information to minimize criticism of Israel by noting that no court has ruled on genocide claims and attributing casualty figures as coming from parties involved in the conflict.

The broader campaign, financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government and routed through European advertising firm Havas Media, aims to manipulate how AI systems respond to user queries. While Piro Inc, the American production company distributing the material, was paid $1 million, Clock Tower X received $15 million and other contractors received millions more. Israeli officials have expressed doubts about the campaign's effectiveness, with some calling it a waste of money as American public opinion has shifted sharply against Israel. Research analysts warn that the most concerning aspect is getting material into AI training data repositories, where false narratives could be regurgitated without citation or fact-checking.
